headline: High: Devin can write shared repo/Slack/Jira/Notion state while Copilot edits repo context, creating dangerous default-path conflicts and cascading trust errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Devin can ingest and act on shared integrations like GitHub PRs and Slack threads, while Copilot reads repo context and editor buffers. That creates a plausible instruction-hijack path if Devin forwards untrusted content into files or chat that Copilot then treats as guidance. No direct clipboard/shared-shell bridge is documented, so medium is the higher justified level.
conditions: IF Devin writes attacker-controlled text into repo files or PR comments that Copilot later consumes as context, injection is possible.
IF Copilot Workspace or chat treats repository text as instructions, the bridge becomes exploitable.
mitigations: Restrict Devin to a dedicated branch and disable PR-comment ingestion for Copilot workflows.
Add a human review step before Copilot acts on Devin-authored text.
Use a prompt-injection filter on any Devin output copied into repo docs or issues.
Separate chat/issue channels from code-context channels where possible.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Devin touches source code, issue trackers, team chat, docs, and secrets like deploy keys and integration tokens; Copilot touches source code and open editor buffers and can access GitHub repo context. Even without a shared host filesystem, the pair can expose sensitive repo or chat content to Copilot’s backend through editor context, so the default blast radius includes sensitive data.
conditions: IF Devin opens secrets-bearing files or chat transcripts in the shared repo context, Copilot can receive them as editor/repo context.
IF the workspace contains sensitive code or tokens, Copilot may process them through its vendor API.
mitigations: Remove secrets from any files visible to Copilot before opening the workspace.
Use secret-scanning and redaction in the repo before pairing the agents.
Limit Copilot to non-sensitive subdirectories or branches.
Keep Devin’s integration tokens out of files and issue text.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Devin has broad shell, filesystem, network, and git write access in a cloud workspace; Copilot Workspace can propose and apply edits with git write capability in the repo context. Both can modify the same codebase, and neither profile shows locking or coordination primitives, so concurrent writes can overwrite each other or corrupt git state in default collaborative use.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same branch or files concurrently, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF Copilot Workspace applies edits while Devin is modifying the same repo state, git corruption or lost work is possible.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch or directory.
Pause one agent while the other is applying edits.
Require a merge/rebase check before any commit lands.
Use file-level ownership rules for hot paths.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Devin operates autonomously inside its workspace, and Copilot Workspace proposes and applies edits for human review. If Devin’s output is fed into Copilot’s context, Copilot may render or act on incorrect facts without a strong verification boundary. The pair therefore supports a default cascade from one agent’s mistakes into the other’s code changes.
conditions: IF Devin-generated summaries or code are used as authoritative input to Copilot Workspace, errors can propagate into edits.
IF human review is skipped or superficial, the cascade reaches committed code.
mitigations: Require explicit source links for any Devin-produced claim before Copilot uses it.
Add a verification checklist before Copilot applies edits from Devin output.
Keep Devin outputs in a separate review queue, not directly in repo context.
Block auto-apply when the input originated from another agent.

E_compliance.rationale: Devin handles team chat, issue trackers, docs, and integration tokens, while Copilot is tied to GitHub repo and chat context. That creates a plausible retention/residency mismatch across collaboration data classes, but the profiles do not show a specific jurisdictional breach or regulated-data class like PHI. Medium fits because policy mismatch is plausible in default use, though not proven.
conditions: IF the workspace contains EU PII or other regulated data, differing vendor handling policies may create a compliance gap.
IF retention or deletion requests must be honored across both vendors, mismatched policies can block fulfillment.
mitigations: Inventory data classes before pairing the agents.
Avoid placing regulated data in shared repo context.
Align retention settings and deletion workflows across vendors.
Document which system is source of truth for each data class.
